# 1.4 - Reading Box Plots and Outliers {.unnumbered}

Nine students ride the bus to school. Eight of them ride from 12 to 22 minutes. One student rides 45 minutes.

Is 45 just a long ride, or is it far away from the rest? Statistics has a rule to decide.

In this lesson, you read box plots, compare two box plots, and find {{< glink slug="outlier" text="outliers" >}}.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I read the five-number summary from a box plot.
- [ ] I tell what percent of the data is in each part of a box plot.
- [ ] I compare two box plots.
- [ ] I use the 1.5 × IQR rule to find outliers.
:::

### 1.4.1 - Reading a Box Plot

This box plot shows the test scores of a class.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_box_plot_scores.svg){width="560px" fig-align="center"}

Each of the 4 parts holds about **25%** of the data.

| Part of the box plot | Percent of the data | What it means here |
|---|:---:|---|
| The box (Q1 to Q3) | 50% | Half of the students scored from 68 to 84. |
| Above Q1 | 75% | About 75% scored more than 68. |
| Below the median | 50% | Half scored less than 76. |

:::{.gotcha title="A long part does not mean more data"}
The right whisker (84 to 98) is long. It still holds only about 25% of the students. A long part means those scores are **spread out**.
:::

***

### 1.4.2 - Comparing Box Plots

Put both box plots on the **same number line**. Then compare the centers and the spreads.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_compare_classes.svg){width="560px" fig-align="center"}

| | Morning | Afternoon |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Center (median) | 72 | 78 |
| Spread (IQR) | $80 - 65 = 15$ | $82 - 70 = 12$ |

The afternoon class scored **higher** (larger median). The afternoon scores are also **closer together** (smaller IQR).

***

### 1.4.3 - Outliers

An {{< glink outlier >}} is a value far away from the rest of the data.

:::{.remember title="The 1.5 × IQR Rule"}
1. Find Q1, Q3, and the IQR.
2. Lower fence $= Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$
3. Upper fence $= Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$
4. A value below the lower fence or above the upper fence is an **outlier**.
:::

**Example:** 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 30

Q1 = 8.5, Q3 = 13.5, and IQR = 5.

$$
1.5 \times 5 = 7.5
$$

$$
\text{Lower fence} = 8.5 - 7.5 = 1 \qquad \text{Upper fence} = 13.5 + 7.5 = 21
$$

30 is above 21, so **30 is an outlier**. 3 is not below 1, so 3 is not an outlier.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_outlier_example.svg){width="560px" fig-align="center"}

On a box plot, an outlier is a **dot**. The {{< glink whisker >}} stops at the last value that is not an outlier. Here, that is 14.

:::{.you-try-m title="Is there an outlier?"}
Q1 = 20, Q3 = 30. Is 48 an outlier?
:::
:::{.answer title="Answer"}
IQR $= 30 - 20 = 10$. Upper fence $= 30 + 1.5 \times 10 = 30 + 15 = 45$.

48 is above 45, so **48 is an outlier**.
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Reading Box Plots**

1. This box plot shows how many minutes some students exercise each day.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_box_plot_exercise.svg){width="520px"}

   a. Write the five-number summary.

   b. Find the IQR.

   c. Find the range.

   d. About what percent of the students exercise more than 20 minutes?

   e. About what percent of the students exercise from 35 to 70 minutes?

2. These box plots show how many hours students in two classes use their phones each day.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_box_plots_phone.svg){width="560px"}

   a. Which class has the higher median?

   b. Find the IQR of each class.

   c. Which class is more **consistent** (the values are closer together)? Explain.

   d. About what percent of Class B uses the phone more than 4 hours a day?

***

**Outliers**

3. Nine students recorded how many minutes they ride the bus to school.

   12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 45

   a. Find Q1, Q3, and the IQR.

   b. Find the lower fence and the upper fence.

   c. Are there any outliers? Explain.

4. Ten students timed how many minutes they took to finish a quiz.

   23, 45, 20, 27, 2, 24, 21, 28, 18, 25

   a. Find Q1, the median, Q3, and the IQR.

   b. Find the fences. Which values are outliers?

   c. Make a box plot. Show each outlier as a dot.

5. This box plot shows the points scored by players on a basketball team.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.4_box_plot_points.svg){width="520px"}

   a. What is the maximum?

   b. Find the IQR.

   c. Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to show that 40 is an outlier.

   d. Why does the whisker stop at 22?

***

**True or False**

6. Look at the exercise box plot in problem 1. Is each statement true or false? Explain.

   a. About half of the students exercise from 20 to 45 minutes each day.

   b. The right whisker is the longest part, so most students are in that part.

   c. The mean is 35 minutes.

   d. At least one student exercises exactly 70 minutes.
